items.stem: From which of the following countries Giuseppe Garibaldi belonged to?
items.answer: Giuseppe Garibaldi was an Italian revolutionary and freedom fighter. In 1860 he led his volunteers, the Red Shirts, into southern Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, and handed the conquered territory to Victor Emmanuel II. He belonged to Italy.

Reason (R) : A large part of the Balkan was under the control of Ottoman Empire.
items.assertion: The most serious source of nationalist tension in Europe after 1871 was Balkan.

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Both, (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

items.answer: After 1871 the Balkans became the most explosive region in Europe. Much of it lay under a weakening Ottoman Empire, and as Ottoman power receded the Slavic peoples of the region fought one another and drew in the big powers. The Ottoman grip is exactly why the Balkans became the source of tension, so both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

items.answer: Between 1864 and 1871 Prussia fought three wars, against Denmark, against Austria and against France. All three ended in Prussian victory, and the last was followed by the proclamation of the German Empire. The countries were Austria, Denmark and France.

The revolt was because the contractors did not pay their dues.

items.stem: Which one of the following was not included in the 'Napoleonic Code' of 1804 ?
items.answer: The Civil Code of 1804 did away with all privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property. Since it abolished birth privilege rather than including it, the answer is privilege based on birth.

items.stem: Which of the following revolutions is called as the first expression of nationalism?
items.answer: The French Revolution of 1789 transferred sovereignty from the monarchy to a body of French citizens and created a set of measures, a new flag, a common language, a single system of weights and measures, that made the French a nation. It is called the first clear expression of nationalism.

items.stem: Why was Otto von Bismarck considered as the chief architect of German unification ? Choose the correct option from the following:

items.stem: What did Napoleon do to make the system efficient and rational in France?

items.stem: How did the ‘Treaty of Constantinople’ of 1832 recognize Greece as an independent nation? Explain.
items.answer: The Treaty of Constantinople was signed in August 1832 and it recognised Greece as an independent nation. The Great Powers ratified the treaty and fixed the terms concerning the border between Greece and the Ottoman Empire, ending the war between the Ottomans and the Greeks and granting recognition to Greek independence. The withdrawal of Leopold from the throne of Greece was the instrumental event that led to the signing of this treaty in the presence of officials of Great Powers like Britain and France. Thus the treaty established Greece as an independent nation.

items.stem: Why did Europeans flee to America in nineteenth century ? Explain.
items.answer: During the nineteenth century conditions in Europe were such that people fled to America in large numbers. Poverty and hunger were common, cities were crowded and deadly diseases were widespread. Religious conflicts were common and religious dissenters were persecuted. By the eighteenth century plantations worked by slaves captured in Africa were growing cotton and sugar for European markets, which drew Europeans across the Atlantic. These pressures together drove Europeans to America.

items.stem: Why were big European powers met in Berlin in 1885?
items.answer: All the major European states were invited to the Berlin Conference of 1885, which was organised by Otto von Bismarck, the first Chancellor of Germany. The European powers met to decide the carving up of Africa among themselves. The states taking part were Germany, Spain, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, France and Great Britain, and no African was invited to the conference. So the big powers met at Berlin in 1885 to divide Africa between themselves.

items.stem: The French used school textbooks in Vietnam to justify colonial rule. Explain.
items.answer: The French used school textbooks in Vietnam to glorify themselves and justify colonial rule. The Vietnamese were represented in the textbooks as primitive and backward. They were shown as capable of manual labour but not of intellectual reflection; they could only work in the fields but not rule themselves, and were called ‘skilled copyists’ but not creative. School children were told that only French rule could ensure peace in Vietnam. In this way the textbooks presented colonial rule as necessary and beneficial.

items.stem: Describe any three consequences of liberal revolution of 1848.
items.answer: Three consequences of the liberal revolution of 1848 were: it provided a base for the unification of Germany and Italy; it abolished serfdom and bonded labour both in the Habsburg dominions and in Russia; and the Habsburg rulers granted more autonomy to the Hungarians.
items.ocr: Answer begins on page 18 and finishes at the top of page 19.

items.stem: Which values are attached to a national state?
items.answer: The values attached to a national state are: sacrifices for the nation; pride in the nation's past and present; respect for the national anthem and the national flag; and pride in the nation's brave personalities.

items.stem: Describe main characteristics of Bismarck and his political policy.
items.answer: Bismarck was a great statesman, a conservative, a member of the Prussian Diet, leader of the ruling group and Prime Minister to the king of Germany in 1861. The main characteristics of his political policy were that he was a staunch enemy of liberals and liberalism; he opposed democracy and supported monarchy; and he contributed considerably to the unification of Germany, his ‘Blood and Iron’ policy becoming famous through his strengthening of the military power of the state.

items.stem: What were the impacts of Act of Union Scotland ?
items.answer: The impacts of the Act of Union on Scotland were the formation of the United Kingdom of Great Britain, the dominance of English members in the British Parliament, and the suppression of Scotland's distinctive culture and political institutions.

items.stem: Write short note on the role of economists in awakening of nationalism.
items.answer: Economists began to think in terms of the national economy. They talked of how the nation could develop and what economic measures could bind the nation together. Friedrich List, Professor of Economics at the University of Tubingen in Germany, wrote that a free economic system is the only means to engender national feelings. In this way economic thinking helped awaken nationalism.

items.stem: Explain in short how Ireland was incorporated into United Kingdom in 1801.
items.answer: Ireland was a country divided between Catholics and Protestants. The English helped the Protestants of Ireland to impose their dominance over the Catholics, who were in the majority there. The Catholics revolted against British (Protestant) dominance but were brutally suppressed. The last bid of revolt was organised by Wolfe Tone and his United Irishmen in 1798, and their efforts also failed. Thus Ireland was forcibly incorporated into the United Kingdom in 1801 C.E.

items.stem: Explain the role of women in the nationalist struggles of Europe of the liberals.
items.answer: Women played an active part in the nationalist struggles of the liberals. They formed their own political associations, founded newspapers and took part in political meetings and demonstrations. However, they were still denied the right to vote, and they could not enter the Frankfurt Parliament as representatives but attended only as observers.

items.stem: ‘The issue of extending political rights to women was a controversial one within the liberal movement, in which large numbers of women had participated actively over the years.’ Explain the statement with the help of suitable examples.
items.answer: The issue of extending political rights to women was indeed controversial within the liberal movements, in which large numbers of women had participated actively over the years. Though women had formed their own political associations, published newspapers and taken part in political meetings and demonstrations, they were denied suffrage. When the Frankfurt Parliament convened in the Church of St. Paul, women were admitted only as observers and had to stand in the visitors' gallery. So liberal men welcomed women's participation but resisted their political rights.

items.stem: Write any three values which are considered very important in democratic structure but are suppressed in monarchy.
items.answer: The following values are suppressed under monarchy or despotic rule but are prized in a democratic set-up: personal freedom; the right to equality; the right to express one's opinion freely; and equality before law.
items.ocr: Question asks for three values; the printed answer lists four.

items.stem: Explain any three features of Frankfurt Parliament.
items.answer: Three features of the Frankfurt Parliament were: in the German region a large number of political associations came together in the city of Frankfurt and decided to vote for an all-German National Assembly; on 18th May 1848, 831 elected representatives marched in a festive procession to take their places in the Frankfurt Parliament convened in the Church of St. Paul; and they drafted a Constitution for a German nation to be headed by a monarch subject to a Parliament.

items.stem: Who founded ‘Young Italy’ an when ? Write about it in brief.
items.answer: Giuseppe Mazzini founded ‘Young Italy’ in 1832 in the city of Marseilles in France. It was a new party meant to carry out revolutionary work in Italy. Branches of this party were set up all over Italy with 50,000 members dedicated to the cause of the unification of Italy, and its motto was “God, People and Italy”.

items.stem: Write short notes on Zollverein and Romanticism.
items.answer: Zollverein was a customs union formed in 1834 to abolish tariff barriers and reduce the number of currencies from over thirty to two. It created a wave of economic nationalism and thus strengthened the wider nationalist sentiment. Romanticism was an artistic, literary and intellectual movement that originated in the 18th century to develop a particular form of nationalist sentiment; it glorified folk art and vernacular language.

items.stem: Write the characteristics of European nationalism which emerged after 1830s.
items.answer: Nationalism in Europe after the 1830s had these characteristics: a sense of unity, that people belonged to one country and shared a common history, language and culture; it developed into extreme nationalism through romantic imagination and national feeling; and it was neither exclusive nor chauvinistic.

items.stem: What do you understand by the following two concepts : (1) Conservatism (2) A Modern State
items.answer: Conservatism was a political philosophy that stressed the importance of tradition, established institutions and customs, and preferred gradual development to quick change; it was generally considered a negative philosophy and some people condemned it as an enemy of progress. A Modern State relates to a centralised power that exercises sovereign control over a clearly defined territory, for example the modern U.K. and France.

items.stem: Explain the significance of portraying nations as female figures by the European artists of the 18th and 19th centuries.
items.answer: Since it is difficult to comprehend an abstract idea such as a ‘nation’, artists of the 18th and 19th centuries personified the nation as a female figure. The figure was not the image of any person in real life but a female figure given her own attributes, which came to be an allegory representing the nation. For example Marianne represented the French nation with attributes of liberty such as the broken chain and the red cap, and Germania was imagined as the allegory of the German nation, a female figure wearing a crown of oak leaves which represented heroism.

items.stem: Discuss the role of any two great personalities of Italy in its unification and welfare.
items.answer: Garibaldi was a great patriot, organiser and liberal of Italy. He raised a force named the “Red-Shirts”, whose forces defeated the powerful Austrian forces and liberated Naples and Sicily; after achieving his mission of Italy's liberation and unification this selfless patriot took to the peaceful life of a peasant. Victor Emmanuel was the son of Charles Albert of the royal family of Savoy and was regarded as the body of Italy. He annexed Venetia and Rome (the Papal territories) and thus completed the task of the unification of Italy which Cavour had left incomplete.

items.stem: How was the Habsburg Empire a patchwork of many different regions and peoples in Europe ? Explain.
items.answer: The Habsburg Empire included many regions such as Tyrol, Austria, Sudetenland and Bohemia. The aristocracy spoke German, as did the ruling class in the provinces of Lombardy and Venetia. In Hungary half of the population spoke Magyar and the rest local dialects, while in Galicia the aristocracy spoke Polish. The empire was therefore a patchwork of different regions, peoples and languages held together by a single ruling house.

items.stem: Differentiate between the concept of a modern state and a nation state. How did the sense of common identity develop in Europe ?
items.answer: In a modern state a centralised power exercised sovereign control over a clearly defined territory, and such states had been developing over a long period of time in Europe. A nation state was one in which the majority of its citizens, and not only its rulers, came to develop a sense of common identity and shared history or descent. This commonness was forged through struggles and through the actions of leaders and of the common people; it did not exist from time immemorial.

items.stem: The artist has portrayed Garibaldi as holding on to the base of the boot, so that the King of Sardinia-Piedmont can enter it from the top. Look at the map of Italy once more. What statement is this caricature making?
items.answer: In the picture the boot epitomises the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, which remained in Southern Italy. Garibaldi succeeded in gaining these kingdoms and subsequently handed them over to the king of Sardinia-Piedmont, Victor Emmanuel II, who was proclaimed emperor of united Italy. The caricature therefore states that it was Garibaldi who won the south and gave it to the monarchy, so that the picture shows the role played by Garibaldi in unifying Italy.

items.stem: Explain the measures and practices introduced by the French revolutionaries to create a sense of collective identity amongst the French people.
items.answer: The French revolutionaries took several deliberate steps to build a collective identity among the French people. The ideas of la patrie (the fatherland) and le citoyen (the citizen) were promoted, emphasising a united community enjoying equal rights under a constitution. A new French flag, the tricolour, replaced the royal standard. The Estates General was renamed the National Assembly and was elected by a body of active citizens. New hymns, oaths and martyrs were commemorated in the name of the nation. A central administrative system framed uniform laws for the entire nation. Regional dialects were discouraged and French was promoted as the common language of the nation. Together these measures turned the subjects of a king into citizens of a nation.

items.stem: “Like Germany, Italy too had a long history of political fragmentation”. Explain.
items.answer: It is true that Italy had a long history of political fragmentation. Italians were scattered over several dynastic states, and Sardinia-Piedmont was ruled by an Italian princely house while other regions were under foreign or papal rule. Italy was unified only in 1861, when Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed King of united Italy. Before that, Giuseppe Mazzini had sought to put together a programme for a unitary Italian Republic, and the unification finally came through a series of wars, a tactful diplomatic alliance with France arranged by Chief Minister Cavour, and Garibaldi joining the fray. So Italy, like Germany, remained a patchwork of separate states until the middle of the nineteenth century.

items.stem: How did Greek war of independence mobilise nationalist feelings among the educated elite across Europe? Explain.
items.answer: The Greek war of independence stirred nationalist feeling among educated Europeans in several ways. Greek nationalists received support from Greeks living in exile. Many western Europeans felt a natural sympathy for the Greek cause because of their admiration for ancient Greek culture. Greece was seen as a part of Europe that had been annexed by the Ottomans and now needed to be liberated. Poets and artists treated Greece as the cradle of European civilisation, and this raised nationalist consciousness across the continent. Finally, the Treaty of Constantinople of 1832 recognised Greece as an independent nation, which showed that a nationalist struggle could succeed.

items.stem: Why did merchants moved to the countryside Europe during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries ? Explain.
items.answer: In the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries merchants from the towns of Europe began moving into the countryside, supplying money to peasants and artisans and persuading them to produce for an international market. They did so because the urban crafts and trade guilds were powerful and did not allow merchants to expand production within the towns. These guilds were associations of producers that trained craftspeople, maintained control over production, regulated competition and prices, and restricted the entry of new people into the trade. Rulers also granted individual guilds monopoly rights to produce and trade in specific products. It was therefore difficult for new merchants to set up business in towns, and so they turned to the countryside.

items.stem: How had Napoleonic code exported to the regions under French control? Explain with examples.
items.answer: The Napoleonic Code was carried into the regions under French control along with French rule. It did away with all privileges based on birth, established equality before the law, secured the right to property and abolished feudal dues. Although Napoleon had destroyed democracy in France by returning to monarchy, in the administrative field he incorporated revolutionary principles to make the system more rational and efficient. In the Dutch Republic, Switzerland, Italy and Germany he simplified administrative divisions, abolished the feudal system and freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues. In the towns guild restrictions were removed and transport and communication were improved. Peasants, artisans, workers and new businessmen enjoyed a new-found freedom, and businessmen in particular welcomed uniform laws, standardised weights and measures and a common national currency, which eased the movement of goods and capital from one region to another.

items.stem: How did the local people in the areas conquered by the Napoleon react to France rule ? Explain.
items.answer: Napoleon conquered France, Poland, Switzerland, Italy and Germany and converted the democracy of these countries into a royal living standard. In 1804 he made a constitution known as the Napoleonic Constitution, which brought several changes into the life of the people. The local people reacted against him for three main reasons: the load of taxes was increased on the people, an enquiry was set up over newspapers, and young men were compelled to take up jobs in the military. On the basis of these grievances the public came to see Napoleon as their enemy. In the later period the armies of Britain, Russia, Prussia and Austria fought together against Napoleon at the battle of Waterloo, where he was defeated; he died on the island of Saint Helena.

items.stem: Why did the achievement of national unity in Germany and Italy not result in the establishment of republics in these countries?
items.answer: Although unification took place in both Germany and Italy, republics were not established there. The people of both countries wanted freedom from foreign rule, not from their own kings, and the kings of both countries were quite popular among their people. The Prime Ministers of both countries were the main figures in the unification, but both were loyal to their kings and were not in favour of establishing republics. The leaders of both countries also believed that their interests would be better safeguarded by their own monarchs, and they were not in favour of harming the kings. On the contrary, they helped to restore and strengthen their national monarchies, so unification produced strong monarchies rather than republics.

items.stem: Which social groups came in the forefront in bringing socio-political change in the continent of Europe ? Answer the question by examining their role in the national movement in Europe.
items.answer: The new social groups thrown up by industrialisation came to the forefront of socio-political change in Europe. During the process of industrialisation new social groups came into existence — the working class, and a middle class drawn mainly from industrialists, traders and people engaged in the service sector. Up to the last decades of the nineteenth century the size of these new social groups in mid and Eastern Europe was still limited. After the privileges of the elite classes of Europe came to an end, ideas of unity became popular among the educated and liberal middle classes of the whole continent. It was therefore the educated liberal middle class that led the national movement in Europe.

items.stem: Why was the decade of 1830s known as great economic hardship in Europe? Explain any three reasons.
items.answer: The book answers this question through the nationalist upheaval of the 1830s. A sense of unity developed through a cultural movement bearing nationalist sentiment, in which artists and poets focussed on emotions, intuition and mystical feelings and tried to create a sense of shared heritage and a common cultural past as the basis of the nation. Nationalist movements became aggressive because the monarchies would not accept their demand for republics with political rights and freedom of speech, as in Germany, France and Italy, and the frequent repressive measures left the revolutionaries deeply upset. Diplomatic alliances were formed and several tactics were tried to establish republics, but under monarchy it was difficult to bring democracy into full shape because conservatism pervaded the whole of Europe. These conditions made the 1830s a decade of hardship and unrest in Europe.

items.stem:
Which three ideas of French Revolution inspire the democratic all over the world ? Write about these ideas in brief also.
or
Name and explain those three major principles of 18th century Europe, which influenced almost the entire world.
items.answer: The three ideas are liberty, equality and fraternity. Liberty means freedom of speech and expression; it is the most important political pillar of democracy, and in a democracy the right to liberty is granted to all citizens. Equality means being equal; after liberty it is the second most important principle of democracy, because every citizen is considered equal and discrimination on the basis of gender, colour, religion, region or status is rejected. Fraternity means brotherliness; it strengthens the mutual relations between people, promotes love, affection and co-operation among the people of a nation, and so helps democracy succeed. Liberty, equality and fraternity are therefore the three ideas of the French Revolution that inspired democracies all over the world.

items.stem: Describe the events of French Revolution which had influenced the people belonging to other parts of Europe.
items.answer: Several events of the French Revolution influenced people in other parts of Europe. The political and constitutional changes that came in the wake of the Revolution transferred sovereignty from the monarchy to the National Assembly, a body of French citizens. The Revolution proclaimed that it was the people who would henceforth constitute the nation and shape its destiny. When news of these events reached the cities of Europe, students and other members of the educated middle classes began setting up Jacobin clubs; their activities and campaigns prepared the way for the French armies that moved into Holland, Belgium, Switzerland and much of Italy in the 1790s. With the outbreak of the revolutionary wars, the French armies began to carry the idea of nationalism abroad.

items.stem: Explain with examples the three barriers that are responsible to economic growth in Vietnam.
items.answer: There were several barriers to economic growth in Vietnam. The high level of population hindered the growth of the country. Low agricultural productivity was another barrier; to reduce rural poverty and raise productivity it was necessary to carry out land reforms as the Japanese had done in the 1890s, but sufficient employment could not be generated as expected. There was extensive indebtedness among the peasants because of a lack of funds. Finally, the French colonialists did little to industrialise Vietnam, and in the rural areas landlordism spread and the standard of living declined. These conditions together held back economic growth in Vietnam.

items.stem: Who was Count Camilo De Cavour ? Mention any two of his contributions.
items.answer: Cavour was the Chief Minister of the kingdom of Piedmont and Sardinia. His main aim was to emancipate Italy from Austria, and he led the movement of Italian unification through tact and diplomacy. Through a tactful diplomatic alliance with France arranged by him, Sardinia-Piedmont defeated the Austrian forces in 1859. This defeat of Austria paved the way for the unification of Italy.

items.stem: Mention any two economic obstacles that the liberal nationalists wanted to overcome ? In what ways did the Zollverein customs union of 1834 try to overcome these shortcomings ?
items.answer: The economic obstacles the liberal nationalists wanted to overcome were the absence of freedom of markets, state-imposed restrictions on the movement of goods and capital, and the time-consuming calculations forced on traders by the differences in currency, weights and measures among the thirty-nine states. The Zollverein customs union of 1834 tried to overcome these shortcomings: it was an initiative of Prussia joined by most of the German states, it abolished tariff barriers, it reduced the number of currencies, and it was accompanied by the creation of a network of railways. In this way the Zollverein created a single economic space out of a divided Germany.

items.stem: “Nationalism spreads when people begin to believe that they are all part of the same nation.” Support the statement.
items.answer: The statement is supported by the way a sense of collective belonging grew in Europe. This sense came partly through the experience of united struggles, and partly through a variety of cultural processes by which nationalism captured people’s imagination. History and fiction, folklore and songs helped to promote nationalism, and literature helped to arouse national feelings. The idea of nationalism also developed through the celebration of regional festivals. As the national movement developed, nationalist leaders made more and more use of icons and symbols to unify people and to inspire in them a feeling of nationalism. Nationalism therefore spread as people came to believe that they shared one nation.

items.stem: Describe any three problems faced by the French in the sphere of education in Vietnam.
items.answer: The French faced several problems in the sphere of education in Vietnam. After receiving western education the Vietnamese might question colonial domination, as Indians had done under British rule, because they would become aware of western democracies and would put forward various demands before the French government. Educated Vietnamese might also demand white collar or better-paid jobs such as those of teachers and policemen, which were being held by the French citizens called colons living in Vietnam, so there was opposition from those French citizens to giving education to the Vietnamese. In addition, the elites in Vietnam were under the powerful influence of Chinese culture, and it was necessary for the French to counter this influence too.

items.stem: What was Frederic Sorrieu’s Utopian vision ? Discuss the three expressions that he depicted in his famous ‘First Print’.
items.answer: In his Utopian vision Sorrieu saw the countries of Europe as nation states, each having its own flag and national costume. In the ‘First Print’ he depicted a procession of people of different groups paying homage to the Statue of Liberty, and this gives the following expressions. The procession is led by the United States, showing that the other countries should also become nation-states like the US and Switzerland. The tricolour flags in the hands of the people of France inspire other countries to make a revolution and become nation-states. The flags of different colours in the hands of the German people show the need for unity. The fourth group, formed by other countries and moving towards the Statue of Liberty, shows the final goal of becoming nation-states. The depiction of Christ, saints and angels symbolises fraternity among the nations of the world.

items.stem: How did Romanticism seek to develop a particular form of nationalist sentiments during 18th century ? Explain.
items.answer: Romanticism refers to a cultural movement which sought to develop a particular form of national sentiment. Romantic artists and poets generally criticised the glorification of reason and science and focussed instead on emotion, intuition and mystical feeling. Their effort was to create a sense of shared collective heritage and a common cultural past as the basis of the nation. Some German romantics believed that the true spirit of the nation could be popularised through folk songs, folk poetry and folk dances, and that German culture was to be discovered among the common people. In this way Romanticism built nationalism out of culture rather than out of reason.

items.stem: Discuss in brief the reaction of the local population against the administrative changes introduced by Napoleon in order to make it more efficient.
items.answer: A mixed reaction was witnessed against the administrative changes enforced by Napoleon. People in states like Holland and Switzerland, and the urban people living in Brussels, Mainz, Milan and Warsaw, welcomed the French armies as harbingers of liberty. On the other hand, the increase in taxation, censorship and forced conscription of youth imposed by Napoleon were criticised, because these measures reduced people’s freedom to a minimum. Administrative changes such as the removal of privileges based on birth, equality before the law, the abolition of feudalism and the removal of guild restrictions could not by themselves appease the people there. So the same reforms that were welcomed at first came to be resented as French control tightened.

items.stem: Explain the process of unification of Itally.
items.answer: Italy was scattered over several dynastic states as well as the multi-national Habsburg Empire. After the failure of the revolutionary uprisings of 1848, King Victor Emmanuel II of Sardinia-Piedmont took upon himself the task of unifying Italy. Sardinia-Piedmont entered into a diplomatic alliance with France and, with French help, succeeded in defeating the Austrian forces in 1859. In 1860 regular troops along with a large number of armed volunteers marched into South Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies and succeeded in driving out the Spanish rulers. In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed the king of united Italy.

items.stem: Why did the achievement of national unity in Germany and Italy not result in the establishment of republics in these countries?
items.answer: Although unification took place in Germany and Italy, republics were not established in these countries. The people of both countries wanted freedom from foreign rule and were not against their own kings, who were quite popular among their people. The Prime Ministers of both countries were the main figures in the unification of their respective countries, but both were loyal to their kings and were not in favour of establishing republics. The leaders of both countries also held that their interests would be better safeguarded by their own kings and were not in favour of harming them; instead they helped to restore and strengthen their national monarchies. Unification therefore ended in strong monarchies rather than republics.

items.stem:
In some scholar’s view, Great Britain was the model of nation or nation-state. Justify the view.
or
How was the formation of nation-state in Britain different from that of rest of the Europe ? Discuss.
items.answer: Unlike Germany, Italy or France, the formation of the nation-state in Britain was not the outcome of any revolution. Before the eighteenth century no British nation-state existed; the British nation was the result of a long and gradual political, cultural and economic process. The Parliament in Britain obtained power from the monarch through a long-drawn ideological conflict, and out of that conflict Britain emerged as a nation-state. A new and enlarged British nation was then forged by propagating English culture in the nearby states, Ireland and Scotland being the examples. Britain is therefore taken as a model of a nation-state formed by gradual growth rather than by revolution.

items.stem: Describe any four dissimilarities between the process of unification of Italy and Germany.
items.answer: The German unification was not supported by armed volunteers, whereas in the Italian unification Garibaldi had won the support of local peasants to drive out the Spanish rulers. No secret societies were formed to achieve the goal of unification in Germany, but in Italy Mazzini formed Young Italy. Italian unification was completed ten years before Germany was united. Germany had to fight against France and Austria for its unification, while in Italy Cavour used a tactful diplomatic alliance with France to defeat Austria. Finally, Bismarck followed the policy of ‘Blood and Iron’ for German unification, while Cavour relied on his excellent diplomatic skills in Italian unification.

items.stem:
Give four examples to explain the way the artists represented a nation in the nineteenth century, in Europe.
or
“The female figure became an allegory of the nation in Europe in the 18th and 19th centuries.” Justify the statement.
items.answer: In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries European artists personified the nation, that is, they represented a nation as a person, and they chose a female figure — not a real woman — to represent it. The female figure itself carried ideas such as liberty, justice and the republic. In France the female figure Marianne represented the idea of the people’s nation, and her figures were marked on coins and stamps. In Germany the same work was done in the form of Germania; there the oak stood for heroic acts, so Germania wore a crown of oak leaves. The female allegory therefore gave the abstract idea of the nation a concrete and recognisable form.

items.stem:
Explain the conditions that were viewed as obstacles to the economic exchange and growth by the new commercial classes during the nineteenth century in Europe.
or
Which conditions were viewed as obstacles to economic exchange and growth by the new commercial classes during Napoleon’s rule ? State.
items.answer: During the nineteenth century Europe faced several great obstacles to economic exchange and growth as seen by the commercial classes. There was an enormous increase in population all over Europe. Population from the rural areas migrated to the cities to live in overcrowded slums and could not afford to fulfil their basic needs. Unemployment increased, and in most countries there were more job seekers than jobs. Cheap machine-made goods from England gave stiff competition to the small producers of European towns. The prices of food inflated many times over because of bad harvests, which led to widespread pauperism in European towns. These conditions together blocked economic exchange and growth.

items.stem:
Describe any five economic hardships faced by Europeans during the mid-nineteenth century.
or
The period between 1830-48 is called the age of revolutions in Europe and characterised by hunger and hardship? Give any five reasons.
items.answer: Europe saw its worst days from 1830 to 1848, when hunger, hardship, revolt and the revolution of the liberals made the economic condition worst, and there was an enormous increase in population all over Europe. There were more seekers of jobs than employment in most of the countries. Small producers in towns were often faced with stiff competition from imports of cheap machine-made goods from England. The textile industry was the most affected by England’s industrialisation. A rise in food prices or a year of bad harvest led to widespread pauperism in towns and villages. The year 1848 was such a year: food shortages and widespread unemployment brought the population of Paris out on the roads and forced Louis Philippe to flee.

items.stem: Through a focus on any two European countries, explain how nations developed over the 19th century.
items.answer: In the nineteenth century nations developed in different ways, as the examples of Italy and Britain show. Italy emerged after the long drawn wars between the forces of Sardinia-Piedmont and those who ruled over the different parts of Italy, such as Austria and Spain; but it was only through the successful diplomatic engineering of Cavour that the military could attain the end result. Britain, on the other hand, had no history of bloodshed. There the one ethnic group, the English, exerted its power over the other ethnic groups — Scottish, Irish and others — of the land. The English abolished their national symbols, political institutions, national dresses and other cultural identities, and made them follow the British flag, national symbol and anthem. Italy was therefore built by war and diplomacy, and Britain by the gradual dominance of one ethnic group over the others.

items.stem: Write any five points to show the importance of Giuseppe Garibaldi.
items.answer: Garibaldi played a central role in the unification of Italy. He headed the armed volunteers who fought for the unification of Italy. The Kingdom of Two Sicilies was ruled over by the Spanish rulers, and Garibaldi wanted to win the support of the local Italian peasant population. In 1860 he marched into South Italy and the Kingdom of Two Sicilies and succeeded in winning the support of the local peasants, and he drove out the Spanish rulers. The peasant masses who had supported Garibaldi in southern Italy had never heard of Italia, and believed that ‘La Talia’ was Victor Emmanuel’s wife. In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed the king of united Italy, a result made possible by Garibaldi’s campaign.

items.stem: Discuss the role of Mazzini, Cavour and Garibaldi in the unification of Italy.
items.answer: Cavour led the movement to unify the regions of Italy, and through a tactful diplomatic alliance with France engineered by him, Sardinia-Piedmont succeeded in defeating the Austrian forces. Garibaldi gathered a large number of armed volunteers and marched into South Italy and the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, and succeeded in winning the support of the locals to drive out the Spanish rulers. Mazzini had sought to put together a coherent programme for a unitary Italian Republic, and had also formed a secret society called ‘Young Italy’ for the dissemination of his goal. The three men together — Mazzini with the idea, Cavour with diplomacy and Garibaldi with arms — brought about the unification of Italy.

items.stem:
How has French artist Frederic Sorrieu, visualised in his first print of the series of his dream of democratic and republic.
or
What do you know about Frederic Sorrieu? Discuss four prints prepared by him expressing his vision.
items.answer: Frederic Sorrieu was a French artist who prepared a series of four prints visualising his dream of a world made up of democratic and social republics. The first print of the series shows the peoples of Europe and America — men and women of all ages and social classes — marching in a long train and offering homage to the Statue of Liberty as they pass by it. The second print is that of the allegory of liberty in a female figure holding the torch of enlightenment in one hand and the Charter of the Rights of Man in the other. The third print is that of the shattered remains of the symbols of absolutist institutions. The fourth print refers to his utopian vision in which the peoples of the world are shown marching together on the path of development; it is a vision of world peace and prosperity.

items.stem: How was a nation visualized in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries in Europe ? Explain with the help of two suitable examples.
items.answer: Artists represented nations as a female figure which did not stand for any particular woman but gave the abstract idea of the nation a concrete form. Female figures thus became an allegory of a nation, and during the French Revolution artists used female figures to portray ideas such as liberty, justice and the republic through symbols. In France she was christened Marianne, underlining the idea of a people’s nation with characteristics drawn from liberty and the republic; her statues were erected in public places to remind people of unity and to persuade them to identify with it, and her images were also marked on coins and stamps. In Germany, Germania became the allegory of the nation, wearing a crown of German oak leaves, as the German oak stood for heroism. Marianne and Germania are therefore the two examples of how a nation was visualised.

items.stem: What is this caricaturist trying to depict?
items.answer: The caricature aims to depict the true character of the conservative monarchies of nineteenth century Europe. As a matter of fact, the ideals of liberalism and individual freedom did not flourish under them. In the picture the thinkers of the club are shown sitting together, but they do not have the power to express their thoughts, as is reflected by the cloth tied over their mouths. This is the most effective way of projecting that the people did not have freedom of thought or of speech in those times.

items.stem: Describe the caricature. How does it represent the relationship between Bismarck and the elected deputies of parliament? What interpretation of democratic processes is the artist trying to convey?
items.answer: In this caricature Bismarck is shown waving a hunting whip in the air before the elected representatives, and the whip is a symbol of autocracy; it demonstrates that the elected representatives of parliament are fearful of him. In order to show him reverence, the representatives have bowed down under the benches of the parliament. The caricature puts Bismarck on a higher pedestal and shows that he is ruling the roost of the parliament. The artist is trying to narrate democracy through a sarcastic caricature: it shows that democracy existed only for the sake of the name, and that in reality the power and influence of Bismarck ruled the parliament.

items.stem: Explain the process of formation of ‘United Kingdom of Great Britain’.
items.answer: There was no British nation before the eighteenth century. The people of the British Isles identified themselves primarily as English, Welsh, Scot or Irish, each group with its own cultural and political traditions. The British nation-state was therefore not the product of a sudden upheaval or revolution but of a long-drawn-out process. As the English nation grew steadily in wealth and power it was able to extend its influence over the other nations of the islands, and the English parliament became the instrument through which a nation-state with England at its centre was forged. The Act of Union of 1707 between England and Scotland created the ‘United Kingdom of Great Britain’, and in 1801 Ireland was forcibly incorporated into the United Kingdom. A new ‘British nation’ was then forged through the propagation of a dominant English culture, its symbols being the English language, the Union Jack and the national anthem, while the older nations survived only as subordinate partners.

items.stem: How did the ideology of ‘liberalism’ affect the Europe in early nineteenth century? Explain.
items.answer: The term liberalism derives from the Latin root liber, meaning free, and in early nineteenth-century Europe it stood for a cluster of political and economic ideas. Politically it meant freedom of the individual and equality of all before the law, the end of autocracy and clerical privilege, and government by a constitution and an elected parliament rather than by an absolute monarch. Its idea of equality was, however, limited: liberals opposed universal adult franchise, and the right to vote was confined to propertied men, with women excluded altogether. Liberalism also stressed the inviolability of private property. In the economic sphere it stood for freedom of markets and the abolition of state-imposed restrictions on the movement of goods and capital, a demand that led directly to the customs union or Zollverein. Liberalism thus gave the middle classes of Europe a programme that combined constitutional government with economic freedom.

items.stem: Why was the period of 1848 considered as phase of the revolution of the Liberals in Europe?
items.answer: The events of February 1848 in France brought about the abdication of the monarch and the proclamation of a republic based on universal male suffrage. In other parts of Europe where independent nation-states did not yet exist — Germany, Italy, Poland and the Austro-Hungarian Empire — men and women of the liberal middle classes combined their demand for constitutionalism with the demand for national unification. They used the growing popular unrest to press for a nation-state founded on parliamentary principles: a constitution, freedom of the press and freedom of association. In the German regions a large number of political associations, whose members were middle-class professionals, businessmen and prosperous artisans, came together at Frankfurt and voted for an all-German National Assembly. The movement failed because the opposition of the aristocracy and the military grew stronger while the assembly, dominated by the middle classes, resisted the demands of workers and artisans and so lost their support; troops were called in and the assembly was forced to disband. The issue of political rights for women also remained unresolved even though women had formed their own political associations, founded newspapers and taken part in meetings and demonstrations. Because the initiative, the demands and the leadership all came from the liberal middle classes, 1848 is called the revolution of the liberals.

items.stem: “The first clear expression of nationalism came with the ‘French Revolution’ in 1789.” Examine the statement.
items.answer: The statement is true. Till 1789 France was a full-fledged territorial state under an absolute monarch, and the political and constitutional changes brought by the French Revolution transferred sovereignty from the monarchy to the body of French citizens. The revolution proclaimed that it was the people who would henceforth constitute the nation and shape its destiny. From the beginning the revolutionaries introduced measures and practices that created a sense of collective identity: a new tri-colour flag replaced the royal standard, the Estates General was elected by the body of active citizens and renamed the National Assembly, new hymns were composed, oaths taken and martyrs commemorated in the name of the nation, a centralised system of administration with uniform laws was framed, internal customs duties and dues were abolished, and a uniform system of weights and measures was adopted. Regional dialects were discouraged and French, as spoken and written in Paris, became the common language of the nation. The revolutionaries further declared that they would help other peoples of Europe to become nations; students and educated middle classes set up Jacobin clubs, and French armies moved into Holland, Belgium, Switzerland and much of Italy in the 1790s. With the outbreak of the revolutionary wars, nationalism spread across Europe.

items.stem: How did a wave of economic nationalism strengthen the wider nationalist sentiment growing in Europe? Explain.
items.answer: In the first half of the nineteenth century Napoleon’s administrative measures had created out of countless small principalities a confederation of thirty-nine German states. Each of these possessed its own currency and its own weights and measures, and duties were often levied according to the weight or measurement of the goods, so that a merchant moving goods across the region had to deal with a bewildering succession of tariffs and standards. The new commercial classes viewed these conditions as obstacles to economic exchange and growth. As a result the Zollverein, a customs union, was formed in 1834 at the initiative of Prussia and was joined by most of the German states. It abolished tariff barriers and created a unified economic territory allowing the unhindered movement of goods, people and capital, and reduced the number of currencies from over thirty to two. It created national unity in economic matters at a time when Germany was politically divided, and accustomed the German states to co-operating with one another without Austria, which was not a member. This was the beginning of German unity: economic nationalism strengthened the wider nationalist sentiment growing among Germans and in Europe generally.

items.stem: “The idealistic liberal-democratic sentiment of nationalism in the first half of the 19th century became a narrow creed with limited ends.” Examine the statement.
items.answer: In the last quarter of the nineteenth century nationalism changed its character. It no longer retained the idealistic liberal-democratic sentiment of the first half of the century but became a narrow creed with limited ends, and nationalist groups became increasingly intolerant of each other and ever ready to go to war. The clearest example of this narrow creed was the Balkans. A large part of the Balkans was under the control of the Ottoman Empire, and with the weakening and disintegration of that empire nationalist tensions emerged in the area as its European subject nationalities broke away and declared independence. The people of the Balkans argued that they had once been independent before foreign powers controlled them, so their object was to regain their lost independence, and each claimed territory that another also claimed. The major European powers, jealous of one another’s influence over the region, intervened in turn. The result was that the rivalries of the European powers and among the Balkan states themselves led to a series of wars in the region and finally to the First World War.

items.stem: “The Habsburg Empire that ruled over Austria-Hungary, was a patchwork of many different regions and people.” Justify the statement with suitable examples.
items.answer: In the mid-eighteenth century there were no ‘nation-states’ in Europe as we know them today. Germany, Italy and Switzerland were divided into kingdoms, duchies and cantons whose rulers held autonomous territories, and Eastern and Central Europe lay under autocratic monarchies within whose territories lived very diverse peoples. These people did not see themselves as sharing a collective identity or a common culture: different languages were spoken and people belonged to different ethnic groups. The Habsburg Empire that ruled over Austria-Hungary is the clearest example of such a patchwork. It included the Alpine regions — the Tyrol, Austria and the Sudetenland — as well as Bohemia, where the aristocracy was predominantly German-speaking. It also included the Italian-speaking provinces of Lombardy and Venetia. In Hungary half the population spoke Magyar while the other half spoke a variety of local dialects, and in Galicia the aristocracy spoke Polish. Besides these dominant groups there lived within the boundaries of the empire a mass of subject peasant peoples — Bohemians and Slovaks to the north, Slovenes in Carniola, Croats to the south and Roumans to the east in Transylvania. Such differences did not easily promote a sense of political unity, and the only tie binding these diverse groups together was a common allegiance to the emperor.

items.stem: How did nationalism develop through culture in Europe? Explain. or Describe the cultural process through which nationalism captured people’s imagination.
items.answer: Culture played an important role in creating the idea of the nation in Europe. Art and poetry, stories and music helped shape and express nationalist feeling. Romanticism, a cultural movement, sought to develop a particular form of nationalist sentiment by criticising the glorification of reason and science and focusing instead on emotions, intuition and mystical feelings, so as to create a sense of a shared collective heritage as the basis of a nation; Eugene Delacroix’s ‘The Massacre at Chios’, for example, appealed to the emotions aroused by the Greek struggle. The German philosopher Johann Gottfried Herder claimed that true German culture was to be discovered among the common people — das Volk — through their folk songs, folk poetry and folk dances, which expressed the true spirit of the nation. Karol Kurpinski celebrated the national struggle through his operas and folk dances. Allegories such as Marianne and Germania gave the nation a concrete visual form. The emphasis on vernacular language and the collection of local folklore recovered an ancient national spirit and carried the nationalist message to large audiences who were mostly illiterate. Culture thus strengthened nationalist feelings across Europe.

items.stem: How did a wave of economic nationalism strengthen the wider nationalist sentiment growing in Europe? Explain.
items.answer: The economic condition of the German-speaking regions in the first half of the nineteenth century made economic unity a nationalist demand. Napoleon’s administrative measures had created, out of countless small principalities, a confederation of thirty-nine states. Each possessed its own currency, weights and measures, and duties were often levied according to the weight or measurement of the goods, so that trade across the region was obstructed at every border. The new commercial classes viewed these conditions as obstacles to economic exchange and growth. Accordingly the Zollverein, a customs union, was formed in 1834 at the initiative of Prussia and was joined by most of the German states. It created a unified economic territory allowing the unhindered movement of goods, people and capital, and it created national unity in economic matters at a time when Germany was politically divided. It accustomed the German states to co-operating with one another without Austria, which never became a member, and it was thus the beginning of German unity. In this way economic nationalism strengthened the wider nationalist sentiments among Germans and in Europe as a whole.

items.stem: Why was the Balkans the most serious source of nationalist tension in Europe after 1871? Explain any four reasons? or Why did nationalist tension emerge in the Balkans? Explain any four reasons.
items.answer: The Balkans became the most serious source of nationalist tension in Europe after 1871 for the following reasons. First, the Balkans was a region of great geographical and ethnic variation, comprising modern-day Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia and Montenegro, whose inhabitants were broadly known as Slavs. Second, a large part of the Balkans was under the control of the Ottoman Empire, and the spread of the ideas of romantic nationalism in the region, together with the disintegration of that empire, made the area very explosive. Third, as the different Slavic nationalities struggled to define their identity and win independence, each claimed on the basis of a supposed past history that it had once been independent but had later been subjugated by foreign powers, so the Balkan area became one of intense conflict and the states were jealous of one another, each hoping to gain more territory at the expense of its neighbours. Fourth, the Balkans also became an arena of big-power rivalry: Russia, Germany, England and Austria-Hungary each sought to counter the hold of the others over the region. These rivalries led to a series of wars in the region and eventually to the First World War.

items.stem: Explain any five social and administrative reforms introduced by Napoleon in the regions under his control.
items.answer: Napoleon abolished the surviving feudal order in the territories he controlled and reformed their social and administrative life. First, he made the administration rational and efficient, replacing the confusing patchwork of local authorities with a uniform system. Second, the Civil Code of 1804, known as the Napoleonic Code, did away with all privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property. Third, he simplified administrative divisions and abolished the arbitrary powers of local rulers. Fourth, in the countryside he abolished the feudal system and freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues. Fifth, in the towns he removed guild restrictions on craftsmen and workers. He also improved transport and communication systems, and introduced a common national currency together with uniform weights and measures across the regions. Merchants and small-scale producers in particular welcomed these measures, which made movement and exchange of goods easier.

items.stem: How was the history of the development of nationalism in England different from the rest of Europe?
items.answer: The pattern of nationalism in England was different in the following ways. The emergence of nationalism there was not the result of a sudden upheaval, revolution or uprising as it was elsewhere in Europe. There was no British nation prior to the eighteenth century; the islands were inhabited by different ethnic groups — English, Welsh, Scots and Irish — each with its own cultural and political traditions. Of these the English group steadily grew in power, wealth and importance and extended its influence over the others. In 1688, through a bloodless revolution, the English parliament seized power from the monarchy and became the instrument that set up a nation-state with England at its centre. By the Act of Union of 1707 Scotland was incorporated into the United Kingdom, and although the Irish Catholics were against a union with England, Ireland was forcibly incorporated in 1801. It was therefore parliamentary action rather than revolution or war that was the instrument through which the United Kingdom was forged into a strong nation-state.

items.stem: What were the similarities between the process of unification of Germany and Italy? Write in detail.
items.answer: The unification of Germany and of Italy resembled each other in several ways. Both countries were divided into a large number of small states which lacked unity. In both, Napoleon Bonaparte indirectly encouraged unification and nationalist feeling by sweeping away the old order. In both, the Vienna Congress of 1815 again divided the countries into smaller states and restored conservative rule. Both suffered under the reactionary policies of Austria and had to fight against Austria to achieve unity. In both, the efforts of revolutionaries in 1830 and 1848 failed, and the unifications were finally accomplished not by the people but by the rulers and their chief ministers — Bismarck in Prussia and Cavour in Piedmont-Sardinia — through diplomacy and war. In both cases the new states became monarchies rather than republics after liberation and unification, and although democratic and revolutionary leaders and ordinary people played a vital part, they remained loyal to their respective kings.

items.stem: Discuss the general characteristics of the nationalist movement in Poland.
items.answer: Poland in the seventeenth century was a fairly large state, but her neighbours Russia, Austria and Prussia were hostile and fought long and bloody wars with her. Poland was partitioned three times — in 1772, 1793 and 1795 — and by 1795 she had ceased to exist as an independent country. Under Czar Nicholas I, a harsh autocrat, the patriotic Poles were mercilessly suppressed, and although Alexander I had granted Poland a constitution, he gave up his liberalism and became a reactionary under the influence of Metternich of Austria. The Polish revolutionaries within Russia began an armed movement, but Nicholas I crushed the revolt of 1830 and about 45,000 Poles were banished from their homeland. In spite of the partitions the Poles kept their national feeling alive through music and language: Karol Kurpinski celebrated the national struggle through his operas and music and turned folk dances such as the polonaise and the mazurka into nationalist symbols. After the failure of the armed rebellion against Russian rule, members of the Polish clergy used language as a weapon of national resistance, using Polish for church gatherings and for all religious instruction, so that the use of Polish came to be seen as a symbol of the struggle against Russian dominance.

items.stem: How did nationalism develop through culture in Europe? Explain. or “Culture has played an important role in the development of nationalism in Europe during eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.” Support the statement with examples.
items.answer: Culture played an important role in creating the idea of the nation: art and poetry, stories and music helped express and shape nationalist feelings, and Romanticism in particular developed a distinctive form of nationalist sentiment. The Romantic artists turned away from the glorification of reason and science and focused on emotions, intuition and mystical feelings, seeking to create a sense of a shared collective heritage and a common cultural past as the basis of a nation. The German philosopher Johann Gottfried Herder tried to popularise the true spirit of the nation through folk songs, folk poetry and folk dances, arguing that true German culture was to be discovered among the common people. The emphasis on vernacular language and the collection of local folklore served both to recover an ancient national spirit and to carry the modern nationalist message to large audiences who were mostly illiterate. In Poland, which had been partitioned by the great powers, national feelings were kept alive through music and language: the use of Polish came to be seen as a symbol of the struggle against Russian dominance, and after the failure of an armed rebellion against Russian rule many members of the Polish clergy used language as a weapon of national resistance, using Polish for church gatherings and for all instruction. In France, likewise, a common language brought a collective identity among the French people.

items.stem: Discuss the characteristics of the nationalist movement in Greece.
items.answer: The Greeks began their war of independence in 1820 against the Ottoman Empire, and the awaited opportunity came in 1821 when Ali Pasha, the Turkish governor of Janina, quarrelled with the Sultan and went to war with him; Prince Hypsilanti was defeated in the battle at Moldavia by the Turks and the movement fizzled out for a short time. The war then developed into one of mutual extermination and was conducted on both sides with the utmost ferocity. For the first six years, from 1821 to 1828, the great powers did not intervene and the Greeks were left to their own efforts, Metternich being against giving help to revolutionaries. Nationalist feelings elsewhere in Europe were nevertheless strengthened by the Greek struggle: poets and artists such as Lord Byron, who organised funds and later went to fight and died of fever there, lauded Greece as the cradle of European civilisation and mobilised public opinion. To prevent independent action by Russia, Metternich induced France and Czar Nicholas I to join England in forcing an armistice on the Sultan. A conference was held in London in July 1827 and a joint note despatched to Turkey to grant autonomy, but the Sultan refused, whereupon the allied fleets of France and England destroyed the Turkish fleet at Navarino on 20 October 1827. By the Convention of London of 1832 the new kingdom of Greece was recognised and placed under the joint guarantee of the powers, and Prince Otto of Bavaria was chosen as its king. Greece thus afforded the first example of the victory of nationalism against the reactionary policy of the Congress of Vienna and struck a blow at Metternich’s system.

items.stem: Describe the process of unification of Germany.
items.answer: After 1848 nationalism in Europe moved away from its association with democracy and revolution, and nationalist sentiment was often mobilised by conservatives to promote state power and political domination. Germany was unified in this way. Thirty-nine German states had been grouped together in an organisation known as the German Confederation. In 1834 a customs union or Zollverein was established, which allowed free trade among its members and created a real national unity in economic matters. In May 1848 a large number of political associations voted for an all-German National Assembly at Frankfurt, which drafted a constitution for a German nation to be headed by a monarchy subject to a parliament; the crown was offered to the Prussian king but he rejected it, and the liberal initiative to nation-building failed. Thereafter the task of unification was taken over by Prussia and its chief minister Otto von Bismarck, who became the architect of modern Germany. Bismarck followed a policy of ‘blood and iron’ and carried out his plans with the help of the Prussian army and bureaucracy: within seven years three wars were fought, with Denmark, Austria and France, and all ended in Prussian victory. Finally, in January 1871, in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles, the Prussian king William I was proclaimed German Emperor, and the unification of Germany was complete.

Ernst Renan, 'What is a Nation?': In a lecture delivered at the University of Sorbonne in 1882, the French philosopher Ernst Renan (1823-92) outlined his understanding of what makes a nation. The lecture was subsequently published as a famous essay entitled ‘Qu’ est-cequ’ une nation?’ (‘What is a Nation?’). In this essay Renan criticises the notion suggested by others that a nation is formed by a common language, race, religion, or territory: ‘A nation is the culmination of a long past of endeavours, sacrifice and devotion. A heroic past, great men, glory, that is the social capital upon which one bases a national idea. To have common glories in the past, to have a common will in the present, to have performed great deeds together, to wish to perform still more, these are the essential conditions of being a people. A nation is therefore a large-scale solidarity… Its existence is a daily plebiscite… A province is its inhabitants; if anyone has the right to be consulted, it is the inhabitant. A nation never has any real interest in annexing or holding on to a country against its will. The existence of nations is a good thing, a necessity even. Their existence is a guarantee of liberty, which would be lost if the world had only one law and only one master.

Questions :

2. Write any two requirements for the formation of a nation.
3. How does a heroic past helps in the formation of a nation?

1. A nation is a country, or all the people who live in a country.
2. Population and territory are two requirements for the formation of a nation.
3. A heroic past gives a people a sense of pride and identity, and this shared pride helps in the formation of a nation.

The Civil Code of 1804 – usually known as the Napoleonic Code – did away with all privileges based on birth, established equality before the law and secured the right to property. This Code was exported to the regions under French control. In the Dutch Republic, in Switzerland, in Italy and Germany, Napoleon simplified administrative divisions, abolished the feudal system and freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues. In the towns too, guild restrictions were removed. Transport and communication systems were improved. Peasants, artisans, workers and new businessmen enjoyed a new-found freedom.

In Western and parts of Central Europe the growth of industrial production and trade meant the growth of towns and the emergence of commercial classes whose existence was based on production for the market. Industrialisation began in England in the second half of the eighteenth century, but in France and parts of the German states it occurred only during the nineteenth century. In its wake, new social groups came into being: a working-class population, and middle classes made up of industrialists, businessmen, professionals.

Following the defeat of Napoleon in 1815, European governments were driven by a spirit of conservatism. Conservatives believed that established, traditional institutions of state and society – like the monarchy, the Church, social hierarchies, property and the family – should be preserved. Most conservatives, however, did not propose a return to the society of pre-revolutionary days. Rather, they realised, from the changes initiated by Napoleon, that modernisation could in fact strengthen traditional institutions like the monarchy.

Questions :
1. What was the core concept of the Napoleonic Code?
2. Who were the new middle class in Europe?
3. What do you meant by conservatism?
items.answer:
1. The Napoleonic Code defined the concept of equality before the law and secured the right to property. It abolished the feudal system and freed peasants from serfdom and manorial dues, and it also brought improvements in the transport and communication system.
2. The growth of industrial production and trade in Europe led to the emergence of commercial classes whose existence was based on production for the market. In its wake new social groups came into being, such as a working-class population and a middle-class population; the middle classes were industrialists, businessmen and professionals.
3. Conservatism is a political philosophy that stressed the importance of tradition, established institutions and customs, and preferred gradual development to quick change.

Ideas of national unity in early-nineteenth-century Europe were closely allied to the ideology of liberalism. The term ‘liberalism’ derives from the Latin root liber, meaning free. For the new middle classes liberalism stood for freedom for the individual and equality of all before the law. Politically, it emphasised the concept of government by consent. Since the French Revolution, liberalism had stood for the end of autocracy and clerical privileges, a constitution and representative government through parliament. Nineteenth-century liberals also stressed the inviolability of private property.

Following the defeat of Napoleon in 1815, European governments were driven by a spirit of conservatism. Conservatives believed that established, traditional institutions of state and society – like the monarchy, the Church, social hierarchies, property and the family – should be preserved. Most conservatives, however, did not propose a return to the society of pre-revolutionary days. Rather, they realised, from the changes initiated by Napoleon, that modernisation could in fact strengthen traditional institutions like the monarchy. It could make state power more effective and strong. A modern army, an efficient bureaucracy, a dynamic economy, the abolition of feudalism and serfdom could strengthen the autocratic monarchies of Europe.

Conservative regimes set up in 1815 were autocratic. They did not tolerate criticism and dissent, and sought to curb activities that questioned the legitimacy of autocratic governments. Most of them imposed censorship laws to control what was said in newspapers, books, plays and songs and reflected the ideas of liberty and freedom associated with the French Revolution. The memory of the French Revolution nonetheless continued to inspire liberals. One of the major issues taken up by the liberal-nationalists, who criticised the new conservative order, was freedom of the press.

1. What is the literal meaning of ‘liberalism’?

3. Why Conservative regimes was characterised by the autocrats?
items.answer:
1. The term ‘liberalism’ is derived from the Latin root liber, meaning free.
2. Conservatives believed that established, traditional institutions of state and society – like the monarchy, the Church, social hierarchies, property and the family – should be preserved.
3. Conservative regimes were autocratic because they did not tolerate criticism and dissent, and sought to curb activities that questioned the legitimacy of autocratic governments.

To be revolutionary at this time meant a commitment to oppose monarchical forms that had been established after the Vienna Congress, and to fight for liberty and freedom. Most of these revolutionaries also saw the creation of nation-states as a necessary part of this struggle for freedom. One such individual was the Italian revolutionary Giuseppe Mazzini, born in Genoa in 1807, he became a member of the secret society of the Carbonari. As a young man of 24, he was sent into exile in 1831 for attempting a revolution in Liguria. He subsequently founded two more underground societies, first, Young Italy in Marseilles, and then, Young Europe in Berne, whose members were like-minded young men from Poland, France, Italy and the German states. Mazzini believed that God had intended nations to be the natural units of mankind.

So Italy could not continue to be a patchwork of small states and kingdoms. It had to be forged into a single unified republic within a wider alliance of nations. This unification alone could be the basis of Italian liberty. Following his model, secret societies were set up in Germany, France, Switzerland and Poland. Mazzini’s relentless opposition to monarchy and his vision of democratic republics frightened the conservatives. Metternich described him as ‘the most dangerous enemy of our social order’. As conservative regimes tried to consolidate their power, liberalism and nationalism came to be increasingly associated with revolution in many regions of Europe such as the Italian and German states, the provinces of the Ottoman Empire, Ireland and Poland. These revolutions were led by the liberal-nationalists belonging to the educated middle-class elite, among whom were professors, schoolteachers, clerks and members of the commercial middle classes. The first upheaval took place in France in July 1830. The Bourbon kings who had been restored to power during the conservative reaction after 1815, were now overthrown by liberal revolutionaries who installed a constitutional monarchy with Louis Philippe at its head. ‘When France sneezes,’ Metternich once remarked, ‘the rest of Europe catches cold.’ The July Revolution sparked an uprising in Brussels which led to Belgium breaking away from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.

Questions :
1. In which place the Italian revolutionary Giuseppe Mazzini was born? Which secret society was joined by Giuseppe Mazzini?
2. What was the basis of Italian unification? When did the first upheaval took place?
3. What is the belief of Mazzini on nation?
items.answer:
1. The Italian revolutionary Giuseppe Mazzini was born in Genoa in 1807 AD. He joined the secret society of the Carbonari.
2. (i) Liberty was the basis of Italian unification. (ii) The first upheaval took place in France in July 1830.
3. Mazzini believed that God had intended nations to be the natural units of mankind.

Read the following extract taken from the textbook and answer the questions that follow :

“A nation is the culmination of a long past of endeavours, sacrifice and devotion. A heroic past, great men, glory, that is the social capital upon which one bases a national idea. To have common glories in the past, to have a common will in the present, to have performed great deeds together, to wish to perform still more, these are the essential conditions of being a people. A nation is therefore a large-scale solidarity ………. Its existence is a daily plebiscite ………. A province is its inhabitants; if anyone has the right to be consulted, it is the inhabitant. A nation never has any real interest in annexing or holding on to a country against its will. The existence of nations is a good thing, a necessity even. Their existence is a guarantee of liberty, which would be lost if the world had only one law and only one master.”

Questions :
1. Explain what Ernst Renan understands should be the attributes of a nation.
2. What do you mean by the concept of ‘modern state’ ? How does it differ from ‘nation-state’ ?
items.answer:
1. According to Ernst Renan the attributes of a nation are : (i) a nation is a large-scale solidarity; (ii) a nation does not annex or hold on to a country against its will; (iii) the existence of a nation is a guarantee of liberty.
2. (i) By a ‘modern state’ we mean a state in which a centralised power exercises sovereign control over a clearly defined territory; in other words, the ruler and the citizens have different identities in a modern state. (ii) The concept of a nation-state differs from that of a modern state in that, in a nation-state, both the citizens and the rulers had a common identity and a shared history. This common identity was established through the struggles of the leaders and the common people.
